stem: Which statement best describes an enzyme?

options.content: A carbohydrate that speeds up reactions in cells
options.rationale: Enzymes are proteins, not carbohydrates.

options.content: A living cell that digests food
options.rationale: Enzymes are molecules made by cells; they are not alive.

options.content: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst
options.rationale: Both key ideas: protein, and catalyst.

options.content: A substance that is used up as it speeds up a reaction
options.rationale: Catalysts, including enzymes, are not used up.

explanation: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts: they speed up the chemical reactions of living things and are not changed by them.

stem: What is a catalyst?

options.content: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not changed by it
options.rationale: This is the definition.

options.content: A substance that slows a chemical reaction down
options.rationale: A catalyst speeds a reaction up.

options.content: A substance that is used up to give energy for a reaction
options.rationale: A catalyst is not used up.

options.content: A product that forms when a reaction is complete
options.rationale: A catalyst is present at the start and is unchanged at the end.

explanation: A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction, so it can be used again. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

stem: True or false: an enzyme molecule is used up when it catalyses a reaction.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. An enzyme is unchanged at the end of the reaction and can catalyse it again and again.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Enzymes are catalysts, so they are not used up.

explanation: Like all catalysts, enzymes are unchanged by the reactions they catalyse. One enzyme molecule can act on many substrate molecules, one after another.

stem: Complete the sentences about how an enzyme works.

payload.template: The substance that an enzyme acts on is called the {{blank:sub}}. It fits into a region of the enzyme called the {{blank:site}}. The substances formed by the reaction are called the {{blank:prod}}.

explanation: The enzyme acts on its substrate, which fits into the active site. The reaction makes the products, which are released.

stem: How is the shape of an enzyme's active site related to the shape of its substrate?

options.content: It is identical to the shape of the substrate.
options.rationale: Two identical shapes would not fit into each other: the shapes are complementary.

options.content: It is complementary, so the substrate fits into it.
options.rationale: They fit together like a lock and its key.

options.content: It is the same shape as the product.
options.rationale: The products no longer fit, so they are released.

options.content: It has no fixed shape and fits any substrate at all.
options.rationale: Then enzymes would not be specific.

explanation: The active site has a shape complementary to the substrate, like a lock and its key. Only a substrate with the right shape fits, which is why enzymes are specific.

stem: Match each enzyme with the reaction it catalyses.

right.content: Fats and oils → fatty acids and glycerol

explanation: Amylase digests starch to maltose, proteases digest proteins to amino acids, lipase digests fats and oils to fatty acids and glycerol, and catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide. Sucrose is broken down by a different enzyme (sucrase), because each enzyme is specific.

stem: Amylase digests starch but has no effect on protein. What does this show about enzymes?

options.content: They are denatured by protein.
options.rationale: Protein does not denature amylase; it simply does not fit the active site.

options.content: They work only at 37 °C.
options.rationale: Temperature is not tested by this observation.

options.content: They are used up by starch, so none is left for the protein.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not used up.

options.content: They are specific: each acts on only one type of substrate.
options.rationale: Only starch fits amylase's active site.

explanation: Enzymes are specific. Starch has a shape complementary to amylase's active site, but protein molecules do not fit, so amylase cannot act on them.

stem: Name the enzyme, found in liver and potato cells, that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

rejected.feedback: Catalase is a catalyst, but the question asks for the name of the enzyme: catalase.

explanation: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide, a poisonous by-product of metabolism, into water and oxygen. It is found in most living cells and is especially active in liver.

stem: In the lock-and-key model of enzyme action, what do the lock and the key represent?

options.content: The lock is the enzyme's active site; the key is the substrate.
options.rationale: The substrate (key) fits into the active site (lock).

options.content: The lock is the substrate; the key is the enzyme.
options.rationale: The substrate fits into the enzyme, not the other way round.

options.content: The lock is the product; the key is the substrate.
options.rationale: The products are released after the reaction; they are not the lock.

options.content: The lock is the enzyme; the key is the product.
options.rationale: The key is the substrate, which fits before the reaction.

explanation: In the lock-and-key model the enzyme's active site is the lock and the substrate is the key. Only a key of the right shape fits, which explains why enzymes are specific.

stem: Tatenda added a small cube of fresh potato to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution in a boiling tube. The mixture fizzed for several minutes and then stopped. Potato cells contain the enzyme catalase.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the gas that was released.

rejected.feedback: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen, not hydrogen.
Carbon dioxide is not a product of this reaction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which test would show that the gas is the one you named?

options.content: It turns limewater milky.
options.rationale: That is the test for carbon dioxide.

options.content: It burns with a squeaky pop.
options.rationale: That is the test for hydrogen.

options.content: It relights a glowing splint.
options.rationale: This is the test for oxygen.

options.content: It turns blue cobalt chloride paper pink.
options.rationale: That is the test for water.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Tatenda then added a second cube of fresh potato, but there was no more fizzing. When he added 5 cm³ more hydrogen peroxide, the fizzing started again. What do these observations show?

options.content: The catalase in the first cube had been used up.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not used up; extra enzyme made no difference.

options.content: The hydrogen peroxide had been used up, not the catalase.
options.rationale: Adding substrate restarted the reaction; adding enzyme did not.

options.content: The second cube of potato contained no catalase at all.
options.rationale: The reaction restarted only when substrate was added, so lack of enzyme was not the problem.

options.content: Hydrogen peroxide is the catalyst in this reaction.
options.rationale: Hydrogen peroxide is the substrate; catalase is the catalyst.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Predict and explain what would happen if the experiment were repeated with a cube of potato that had been boiled for 10 minutes and cooled.

points.description: No (or hardly any) fizzing / no oxygen released
Boiling denatured the catalase: the shape of its active site changed, so hydrogen peroxide no longer fits (no enzyme-substrate complexes form)

parts.explanation: There would be no fizzing. Boiling denatures catalase: the shape of its active site changes, so hydrogen peroxide molecules no longer fit and cannot be broken down.

explanation: Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen, which relights a glowing splint. Adding more enzyme did nothing but adding more substrate restarted the fizzing, so the substrate had run out. Boiled potato gives no fizzing because its catalase is denatured.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Oxygen: $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$.
2. (b) Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
3. (c) Extra enzyme had no effect, extra substrate restarted the reaction: the substrate had been used up.
4. (d) No fizzing, because the catalase was denatured by boiling.
hints: Which was missing when the fizzing stopped: the enzyme or the substrate?

stem: (Supplement) What is an **enzyme-substrate complex**?

options.content: The product formed at the end of the reaction
options.rationale: Products are released from the enzyme after the complex breaks up.

options.content: An enzyme that has been denatured by heat and cannot work
options.rationale: A denatured enzyme cannot form a complex with its substrate.

options.content: The structure formed while a substrate is held in the active site
options.rationale: It forms before the products are made and released.

options.content: Two different enzymes joined together
options.rationale: The complex is one enzyme and its substrate.

explanation: When the substrate fits into the active site, the enzyme and substrate together form an enzyme-substrate complex. The reaction then takes place, the products are released and the enzyme is free to act again.
hints: Which two things are joined in the complex?

stem: (Supplement) Which sequence correctly describes how an enzyme catalyses a reaction?

options.content: Enzyme fits into the substrate's active site → reaction takes place → enzyme and substrate both become products
options.rationale: The active site belongs to the enzyme, and the enzyme does not become a product.

options.content: Products fit into the active site → substrate is released → enzyme is used up
options.rationale: This runs backwards, and enzymes are not used up.

options.content: Substrate fits into the active site → enzyme is used up → products are released
options.rationale: The enzyme is not used up; it can act again.

options.content: Substrate fits active site → complex forms → reaction → products released → enzyme reused
options.rationale: Every step is in the right order, and the enzyme is unchanged.

explanation: The substrate fits into the complementary active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex; the reaction happens; the products are released; and the unchanged enzyme can bind another substrate molecule.
hints: Where is the active site, and what happens to the enzyme at the end?

stem: Why do living organisms need enzymes?

options.content: Without them, metabolic reactions at body temperature would be far too slow.
options.rationale: Enzymes make these reactions fast enough at normal body temperatures.

options.content: Enzymes provide the energy for all the reactions in cells.
options.rationale: Enzymes do not supply energy; respiration releases energy.

options.content: Enzymes raise the body temperature so that reactions can happen.
options.rationale: Enzymes speed reactions up without raising the temperature.

options.content: Enzymes are the raw materials from which all products are made.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not used up, so they are not raw materials.

explanation: Metabolic reactions at about 37 °C would be far too slow without catalysts. Enzymes increase their rates enough to sustain life, without the high temperatures that would damage cells.
hints: What would happen to the rates of reactions in cells without catalysts?

stem: True or false: boiling kills enzymes.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Enzymes are proteins, not living things, so they cannot be killed: boiling denatures them.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Enzymes are not alive; high temperatures denature them by changing the shape of the active site.

explanation: Enzymes are protein molecules, not organisms. Boiling denatures them: the shape of the active site changes permanently, so the substrate no longer fits. The correct word is denatured, not killed.

stem:
Rudo investigated trypsin, a protease. She set up four tubes and kept them at 35 °C for 20 minutes. Egg-white suspension is cloudy because it contains particles of protein.

| Tube | Contents | Result after 20 minutes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Egg-white suspension + trypsin solution | Became clear |
| B | Egg-white suspension + boiled and cooled trypsin solution | Still cloudy |
| C | Starch solution + trypsin solution | A sample turned iodine solution blue-black |
| D | Egg-white suspension + water | Still cloudy |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: In which tube was protein digested?

options.content: Tube A
options.rationale: The cloudy protein particles disappeared.

options.content: Tube B
options.rationale: The trypsin was denatured by boiling, so the suspension stayed cloudy.

options.content: Tube C
options.rationale: Tube C contained starch, not protein.

options.content: Tube D
options.rationale: There was no enzyme in tube D.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the mixture in tube A became clear.

points.description: Trypsin (a protease) digested / broke down the protein (in the egg-white particles)
into smaller, soluble molecules (amino acids / short chains), so no particles were left to make it cloudy

parts.explanation: Trypsin digested the insoluble protein particles into smaller, soluble molecules such as amino acids, so there were no particles left to make the mixture cloudy.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the result in tube C.

points.description: Enzymes are specific: trypsin acts only on protein, so the starch was not digested (iodine blue-black shows starch was still present)
Starch does not fit / is not complementary to the active site of trypsin (no enzyme-substrate complex forms)

parts.explanation: Enzymes are specific. Starch does not have a shape complementary to the active site of trypsin, so it cannot fit and is not digested; the iodine test shows the starch is still there.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What do tubes B and D together show?

options.content: Trypsin can digest starch as well as protein.
options.rationale: Tube C shows that it cannot.

options.content: Egg-white protein breaks down by itself in 20 minutes.
options.rationale: Tube D, with water only, stayed cloudy.

options.content: The protein is digested only when active trypsin is present.
options.rationale: Without enzyme (D) or with denatured enzyme (B), nothing happened.

options.content: Boiling makes trypsin work faster.
options.rationale: Boiled trypsin did not work at all.

explanation: Only tube A, with active trypsin and protein, cleared: the protease digested the insoluble protein into soluble products. Trypsin had no effect on starch because enzymes are specific. Tubes B and D are controls showing that active enzyme is needed.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Tube A: the cloudiness (protein particles) disappeared.
2. (b) Protein digested by trypsin into soluble products.
3. (c) Specificity: starch does not fit trypsin's active site.
4. (d) Without active enzyme there is no digestion.
hints: Which tubes contain protein, and which contain active enzyme?
What is the substrate of a protease?

stem: (Supplement) Explain how an enzyme such as amylase catalyses the breakdown of its substrate, and why it cannot act on other substances such as protein. Use the terms **active site**, **substrate**, **enzyme-substrate complex** and **product**. [5]

points.description: The substrate (starch) fits into the active site of the enzyme
The active site has a shape complementary to the substrate (lock and key)
The substrate is broken down into products (maltose), which are released from the active site
The enzyme is unchanged and can be used again
Other substances such as protein have a different shape, so they do not fit the active site: the enzyme is specific

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Starch, the substrate of amylase, fits into the enzyme's active site, which has a shape complementary to it, like a key in a lock. An enzyme-substrate complex forms and the starch is broken down into the product, maltose, which is released. The amylase is unchanged and its active site can accept another starch molecule. Protein molecules have a different shape, so they do not fit amylase's active site and are not acted on: amylase is specific.

explanation: The substrate fits the complementary active site, an enzyme-substrate complex forms, products are released and the enzyme is reused. Substances of other shapes do not fit, so enzymes are specific.
hints: Describe the steps in order, then explain specificity in terms of shape.

options.content: P only
options.rationale: Manganese(IV) oxide is not a protein, so it is not denatured by boiling and still works.

options.content: P and R only
options.rationale: Catalase in Q was denatured; manganese(IV) oxide is not a protein, so boiling does not affect it.

options.content: P, Q and R
options.rationale: Boiling denatured the catalase in Q.

options.content: Q and R only
options.rationale: Fresh liver (P) contains active catalase and gives plenty of oxygen.

explanation: Catalase is a protein, so boiling denatures it and tube Q gives no oxygen. Manganese(IV) oxide is an inorganic catalyst, not a protein: boiling does not change it, so tube R still releases oxygen, as does the fresh liver in tube P.
hints: Which of the two catalysts is a protein?

stem:
Catalase from yeast was added to some hydrogen peroxide solution, and the total volume of oxygen collected was recorded every minute.

| Time / min | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total volume of oxygen / cm³ | 0 | 16 | 27 | 34 | 38 | 39 | 39 |

Why did the volume of oxygen stop increasing after 5 minutes?

options.content: All the catalase had been used up.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not used up in the reactions they catalyse.

options.content: The oxygen bubbles produced had denatured all of the catalase molecules.
options.rationale: Oxygen does not denature catalase; the reaction slowed as substrate ran out.

options.content: Enzymes can only work for about five minutes before they stop working.
options.rationale: There is no fixed working time; the reaction stops when the substrate runs out.

options.content: All the hydrogen peroxide had been broken down, so no substrate was left.
options.rationale: Without substrate the enzyme has nothing to act on.

explanation: The rate fell steadily (16, 11, 7, 4 and 1 cm³ in successive minutes) as the hydrogen peroxide was used up, and stopped when none was left. The catalase was unchanged: adding more hydrogen peroxide would start the reaction again.
hints: Work out how much oxygen was produced in each minute.
Which is used up in a reaction: the enzyme or the substrate?

stem: Minced liver was added to hydrogen peroxide solution, and 54 cm³ of oxygen was collected in 4 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute.
explanation: Mean rate $= \dfrac{\text{volume of oxygen}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{54}{4} = 13.5\ \text{cm}^3$ per minute.
hints: Divide the volume by the time.

stem: Select **all** the statements that are true of enzymes.

options.content: They are living organisms.
options.rationale: They are molecules made by cells; they are not alive.

options.content: They are used up during the reaction.
options.rationale: Catalysts are not used up.

options.content: They can be used again and again.
options.rationale: They are unchanged by the reaction.

options.content: They only break molecules down and never build them up.
options.rationale: Enzymes also build molecules, e.g. joining glucose to make starch.

options.content: They are proteins.
options.rationale: All enzymes in this syllabus are proteins.

options.content: Each enzyme acts on a specific substrate.
options.rationale: Only substrates of the right shape fit the active site.

explanation: Enzymes are proteins, they are specific, and they are not used up, so they can be reused. They are not alive, and they catalyse building-up reactions (such as making starch or glycogen from glucose) as well as breaking-down reactions.
hints: Two of the wrong statements are common misconceptions about enzymes and living things.

stem: When a maize grain germinates, the growing embryo cannot use the starch stored in the grain directly. Which enzyme makes this food available, and what does it produce?

options.content: Catalase, which breaks starch down into oxygen
options.rationale: Catalase acts on hydrogen peroxide, not starch.

options.content: Lipase, which breaks starch down into fatty acids
options.rationale: Lipase acts on fats and oils.

options.content: Amylase, which breaks starch into maltose, a soluble sugar
options.rationale: Insoluble starch is digested into soluble sugar.

options.content: Protease, which joins glucose molecules together into starch
options.rationale: Proteases digest proteins; they do not make starch.

explanation: Starch is insoluble, so it cannot move to the embryo. Amylase in the germinating grain digests it into maltose, a soluble sugar that is carried to the embryo and used for respiration and growth.
hints: Which enzyme has starch as its substrate?

stem:
Lactase is an enzyme that breaks down lactose, the sugar in milk, into glucose and galactose. Glucose test strips change colour only when glucose is present. A student kept three tubes at 37 °C for 10 minutes and then tested each with a glucose test strip.

| Tube | Contents | Glucose test strip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Milk + lactase solution | Changed colour |
| 2 | Milk + water | No change |
| 3 | Sucrose solution + lactase solution | No change |

Which conclusion is supported by these results?

options.content: Lactase broke the sucrose down into glucose and fructose.
options.rationale: Tube 3 showed no glucose, so sucrose was not broken down.

options.content: Milk contains glucose even before lactase is added.
options.rationale: Tube 2, milk with water, gave no glucose.

options.content: Lactase works only at 37 °C.
options.rationale: Only one temperature was tested, so the results cannot show this.

options.content: Lactase made glucose from lactose but not from sucrose: it is specific.
options.rationale: Tubes 1 and 2 show lactose was broken down; tube 3 shows sucrose was not.

explanation: Glucose appeared only when lactase acted on milk (tube 1); milk alone has no glucose (tube 2), so the glucose came from lactose. Sucrose was not broken down (tube 3) because it does not fit lactase's active site: the enzyme is specific. Nothing was tested at other temperatures.
hints: Compare tube 1 with tube 2, then tube 1 with tube 3.
Does the experiment test any temperature other than 37 °C?

stem:
Chipo cut equal volumes of fresh potato into different forms and put each into the same volume of hydrogen peroxide solution at the same temperature.

| Potato sample | Volume of oxygen in 2 minutes / cm³ |
| --- | --- |
| One cube with sides of 2 cm | 5 |
| The same volume cut into eight cubes with sides of 1 cm | 11 |
| The same volume blended into a paste | 38 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: A cube with sides of 2 cm has a surface area of 24 cm². Calculate the total surface area of the eight cubes with sides of 1 cm.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the eight small cubes released oxygen faster than the single large cube.

points.description: Larger (double) surface area, so more potato cells / more catalase are in contact with the hydrogen peroxide
More collisions between substrate and enzyme / more enzyme-substrate complexes form per minute

parts.explanation: Cutting the cube doubled the surface area, so more potato cells, and more of their catalase, were in contact with the hydrogen peroxide. More substrate molecules could reach active sites each minute, so oxygen was released faster.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The blended paste released oxygen fastest of all. What is the most likely reason?

options.content: Blending makes the potato cells produce much more catalase.
options.rationale: Cells cannot make significant amounts of new enzyme in two minutes, and broken cells cannot make any.

options.content: Blending breaks open the cells, so much more catalase meets the substrate.
options.rationale: The enzyme from inside the cells is exposed to the substrate.

options.content: Blending denatures the catalase.
options.rationale: Denatured catalase would release less oxygen, not more.

options.content: Blending adds oxygen to the potato.
options.rationale: The oxygen collected comes from breaking down hydrogen peroxide.

explanation: Eight 1 cm cubes have a total surface area of $8 \times 6 \times 1^2 = 48\ \text{cm}^2$, twice that of the 2 cm cube, so more catalase meets the substrate and the rate roughly doubles (5 to 11 cm³). Blending breaks the cells open and exposes even more catalase.
workedSolution:
1. (a) One small cube: $6 \times 1 \times 1 = 6\ \text{cm}^2$; eight cubes: $8 \times 6 = 48\ \text{cm}^2$.
2. (b) Twice the surface area, so more catalase is exposed and more enzyme-substrate complexes form per minute.
3. (c) Blending releases the catalase from inside the cells.
hints: Where is the catalase in a piece of potato?
